rows.en: This act moves a question along, and the selection carries things that are not questions. The whole set is refused rather than quietly narrowed to the part that fits, because a set that acted on less than you selected is a set you were not shown.

rows.en: A question cannot be the evidence for its own answer. This write would have it rest on itself, which reads as support and adds nothing anybody outside could check.
rows.note: DEC-260: inquiry-grammar, refusal by its code

rows.en: This write would close a loop: the chain it would join already rests, somewhere further along, on the thing being written. The path is named so the loop can be seen rather than re-derived, and support that circles back is support that rests on nothing.
rows.note: DEC-260: inquiry-grammar, refusal by its code

rows.en: Dividing a question says the team asked one thing when it was really asking two, and that is a judgment about the team's own work. The credential that asked here is an automated one: it may raise questions and gather what they rest on, and may not restructure them. Sign in to divide it.
rows.note: DEC-260: inquiry-grammar, refusal by its code

rows.en: Grounding says some of the reasons behind an answer are strong enough to carry it on their own, and it is the one act here that makes a finding stronger rather than weaker. That decision needs a person behind it, and the credential that asked is an automated one. Sign in to ground it.
rows.note: DEC-260: inquiry-grammar, refusal by its code

rows.en: A leg on another team's finding names that finding and one edition, and nothing else: its grades are that edition's. Correct the leg. Nothing was written.
rows.note: DEC-260: inquiry-grammar, refusal by its code

rows.en: A leg on a standard rests on the text of that law as the team captured it, so the only grade it carries is the one that text earns. A connection, a testimony or a hunch is a different kind of claim. Correct the leg. Nothing was written.
rows.note: DEC-260: inquiry-grammar, refusal by its code

rows.en: A leg on a calculation names the calculation and nothing else: how strong it is comes from the figures it was worked from, so the leg states no grade and names no part of its own. Correct the leg. Nothing was written.
rows.note: DEC-260: inquiry-grammar, refusal by its code

rows.en: A leg on a duty's occurrence names the duty and that one occurrence, and nothing else: how strong it is comes from the law that sets the duty and the dates that started and end it, so the leg states no grade, names no part, and is not listed among the references. Correct the leg. Nothing was written.
rows.note: DEC-260: inquiry-grammar, refusal by its code

rows.en: A leg on a connection the record worked out names that connection and the five facts it was worked out from: what kind it is, its two ends, the date it holds as of, and the method. Its name must be the one those five give, and it states no grade or part of its own: how strong it is comes from the links it was worked out over. Correct the leg. Nothing was written.
rows.note: DEC-260: inquiry-grammar, refusal by its code

rows.en: A leg can record each statement of your project's declared bias that was applied to it: the statement, and what it did, which is one of three things: it lowered the leg's grade (from one letter to a weaker one), it set the leg aside, or it refused an inference.
